claim: Cultured mouse peritoneal macrophages release large numbers of ~30-nm cholesterol-rich particles.
source: Cultured mouse peritoneal macrophages release large numbers of ~30-nm cholesterol-rich particles.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by SEM images throughout the manuscript showing particles of this size.

claim: The particles represent fragments of the plasma membrane that are pulled away and left behind during the projection and retraction of filopodia and lamellipodia.
source: Here, we show that those particles represent fragments of the plasma membrane that are pulled away and left behind during the projection and retraction of filopodia and lamellipodia.
evidence: Supported by correlative live-cell microscopy and SEM showing particles deposited where filopodia/lamellipodia had extended and retracted.

claim: The particles are enriched in proteins found in focal adhesions.
source: Consistent with this finding, the particles are enriched in proteins found in focal adhesions, which attach macrophages to the substrate.
evidence: Supported by proteomic analysis showing focal adhesion proteins in particle preparations.

claim: The release of particles is abolished by blocking cell movement with latrunculin A.
source: The release of particles is abolished by blocking cell movement (either by depolymerizing actin with latrunculin A or by inhibiting myosin II with blebbistatin).
evidence: Demonstrated by SEM showing no particles around macrophages pre-treated with latrunculin A.

claim: The release of particles is abolished by blocking cell movement with blebbistatin.
source: The release of particles is abolished by blocking cell movement (either by depolymerizing actin with latrunculin A or by inhibiting myosin II with blebbistatin).
evidence: Demonstrated by SEM showing no particles around macrophages pre-treated with blebbistatin.

claim: The plasma membrane–derived particles are enriched in 'accessible cholesterol' (a mobile pool of cholesterol detectable with the modified cytolysin ALO-D4).
source: Confocal microscopy and NanoSIMS imaging studies revealed that the plasma membrane–derived particles are enriched in 'accessible cholesterol' (a mobile pool of cholesterol detectable with the modified cytolysin ALO-D4) but not in sphingolipid-sequestered cholesterol [a pool detectable with ostreolysin A (OlyA)].
evidence: Supported by NanoSIMS showing 15N enrichment from [15N]ALO-D4 binding to particles.

claim: The plasma membrane–derived particles are not enriched in sphingolipid-sequestered cholesterol.
source: Confocal microscopy and NanoSIMS imaging studies revealed that the plasma membrane–derived particles are enriched in 'accessible cholesterol' (a mobile pool of cholesterol detectable with the modified cytolysin ALO-D4) but not in sphingolipid-sequestered cholesterol [a pool detectable with ostreolysin A (OlyA)].
evidence: Supported by NanoSIMS showing minimal 13C enrichment from [13C]OlyA binding to particles.

claim: Macrophages must dispose of surplus cholesterol through a process generally referred to as 'cholesterol efflux'.
source: The cholesterol in the debris can be esterified and stored in cytosolic lipid droplets (Brown et al., 1980), thereby avoiding toxicity associated with an accumulation of free cholesterol, but macrophages ultimately must dispose of the surplus cholesterol, a process generally referred to as 'cholesterol efflux' (Rosenson et al., 2012; Tall et al., 2002; Rothblat and Phillips, 2010; Adorni et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on cholesterol efflux.

claim: One mechanism for cholesterol efflux involves transferring free cholesterol to high density lipoproteins (HDL), a process that is facilitated by ABC transporters.
source: One mechanism for cholesterol efflux involves transferring free cholesterol to high density lipoproteins (HDL), a process that is facilitated by ABC transporters (Rosenson et al., 2012; Tall et al., 2002; Rothblat and Phillips, 2010; Yvan-Charvet et al., 2010; Westerterp et al., 2014; Duong et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature.

claim: A deficiency of ABCA1 interferes with cholesterol efflux by macrophages, leading to an accumulation of foam cells in tissues.
source: A deficiency of ABCA1 interferes with cholesterol efflux by macrophages, leading to an accumulation of foam cells (macrophages containing numerous cholesterol ester droplets) in tissues (Brooks-Wilson et al., 1999; Bodzioch et al., 1999; Clee et al., 2001; Rust et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Cultured human monocyte–derived macrophages release 'cholesterol microdomains' (varying in size but as large as several hundred nm) onto the surrounding substrate.
source: Using a cholesterol-specific monoclonal antibody and immunocytochemical approaches, the laboratory of Howard Kruth reported that cultured human monocyte–derived macrophages release 'cholesterol microdomains' (varying in size but as large as several hundred nm) onto the surrounding substrate (Jin et al., 2016; Freeman et al., 2014; Ong et al., 2010; Jin et al., 2015; Jin et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work by Kruth's laboratory.

claim: The release of cholesterol microdomains was reduced by decreasing the expression of ABC transporters.
source: The release of these microdomains was reduced by decreasing the expression of ABC transporters (Jin et al., 2016; Freeman et al., 2014; Jin et al., 2015; Jin et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Large numbers of ~30-nm vesicular particles were released from the plasma membrane of mouse peritoneal macrophages and a mouse macrophage cell line by a process that morphologically resembles 'budding.'
source: Recently, we demonstrated, by scanning electron microscopy (SEM), that large numbers of ~30-nm vesicular particles were released from the plasma membrane of mouse peritoneal macrophages and a mouse macrophage cell line by a process that morphologically resembles 'budding.'
evidence: Refers to prior work by the authors (He et al., 2018).

claim: The plasma membrane–derived particles were enriched in 'accessible cholesterol' (a mobile pool of cholesterol that can be detected by ALO-D4, a modified cholesterol-binding cytolysin).
source: The plasma membrane–derived particles were enriched in 'accessible cholesterol' (He et al., 2018), a mobile pool of cholesterol that can be detected by ALO-D4, a modified cholesterol-binding cytolysin (Gay et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work and definition of ALO-D4.

claim: The cholesterol content of the particles could be increased by loading macrophages with cholesterol or by treating the cells with a liver X receptor (LXR) agonist.
source: The cholesterol content of the particles could be increased by loading macrophages with cholesterol or by treating the cells with a liver X receptor (LXR) agonist, and the cholesterol content of the particles could be depleted with HDL (He et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The cholesterol content of the particles could be depleted with HDL.
source: The cholesterol content of the particles could be increased by loading macrophages with cholesterol or by treating the cells with a liver X receptor (LXR) agonist, and the cholesterol content of the particles could be depleted with HDL (He et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Lawns of ~30-nm particles were present on the substrate surrounding macrophages, generally at the lagging pole of the cell and invariably where we had observed, by live-cell imaging, the extension and retraction of filopodia/lamellipodia.
source: Lawns of ~30-nm particles were present on the substrate surrounding macrophages, generally at the lagging pole of the cell and invariably where we had observed, by live-cell imaging, the extension and retraction of filopodia/lamellipodia (Figure 1, Figure 1—videos 1–2).
evidence: Supported by correlative live-cell microscopy and SEM data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Live-cell imaging revealed that the drug-treated macrophages were unable to project and retract filopodia/lamellipodia.
source: Live-cell imaging revealed that the drug-treated macrophages were unable to project and retract filopodia/lamellipodia (Figure 2—videos 1–6).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging videos showing lack of movement in drug-treated cells.

claim: Both latrunculin A and blebbistatin abolished particle release from 'pre-treatment' macrophages.
source: Both latrunculin A and blebbistatin abolished particle release from 'pre-treatment' macrophages (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by SEM images in Figure 2 showing no particles around pre-treated cells.

claim: In latrunculin A–treated 'post-adherence' macrophages, a circumferential ring of particles was left behind on the substrate as the cell retracted with actin depolymerization.
source: In latrunculin A–treated 'post-adherence' macrophages, a circumferential ring of particles was left behind on the substrate as the cell retracted with actin depolymerization (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by SEM images in Figure 2A showing ring of particles.

claim: Blebbistatin eliminated particle release in post-adherence cells.
source: Blebbistatin eliminated particle release in post-adherence cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by SEM images in Figure 2B showing no particles.

claim: Macrophages treated with vehicle alone (DMSO) released large numbers of particles onto the surrounding substrate.
source: Macrophages treated with vehicle alone (DMSO) released large numbers of particles onto the surrounding substrate (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by SEM images in Figure 2 showing particles around DMSO-treated cells.

claim: After removing the drugs, the morphology of the cells returned to normal and particle release resumed, with numerous particles appearing on the surrounding substrate.
source: As an additional control, macrophages that had been incubated with drugs overnight were washed and incubated for an additional 18 hr without drugs. In the absence of the drugs, the morphology of the cells returned to normal and particle release resumed, with numerous particles appearing on the surrounding substrate (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by SEM images in Figure 2 showing particle release after drug removal.

claim: The lawn of particles around macrophages was enriched in 15N, as revealed by NanoSIMS imaging.
source: The lawn of particles around macrophages, visible by SEM, was enriched in 15N, as revealed by NanoSIMS imaging (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by NanoSIMS images in Figure 3 showing 15N enrichment in particles.

claim: The degree of 15N enrichment was greater in the lawn of particles than on the plasma membrane covering the macrophage cell body or macrophage filopodia.
source: Of note, the degree of 15N enrichment was greater in the lawn of particles than on the plasma membrane covering the macrophage cell body or macrophage filopodia (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 3 graph.

claim: After biotinylating cell-surface proteins of macrophages with Sulfo-NHS-SS-biotin, the lawn of particles surrounding macrophages could be detected with fluorescent streptavidin.
source: First, after biotinylating cell-surface proteins of macrophages with Sulfo-NHS-SS-biotin, the lawn of particles surrounding macrophages could be detected with fluorescent streptavidin (colocalizing with fluorescently labeled ALO-D4, which binds 'accessible cholesterol') (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy images in Figure 4A.

claim: By SEM, streptavidin-conjugated 40-nm gold nanoparticles bound to both macrophages and to the surrounding particles.
source: Also, by SEM, streptavidin-conjugated 40-nm gold nanoparticles bound to both macrophages and to the surrounding particles (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by SEM images in Figure 4B showing gold nanoparticles on particles.

claim: There was no binding of the gold nanoparticles to non-biotinylated macrophages.
source: There was no binding of the gold nanoparticles to non-biotinylated macrophages (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by control SEM images in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: By NanoSIMS analyses, the lawn of particles outside macrophages contained 14N and 32S (as well as accessible cholesterol, detectable with [15N]ALO-D4).
source: Second, by NanoSIMS analyses, the lawn of particles outside macrophages contained 14N and 32S (as well as accessible cholesterol, detectable with [15N]ALO-D4) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by NanoSIMS images in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Proteomic studies on three independent particle and plasma membrane preparations revealed that both were enriched in focal adhesion proteins and cytoskeletal components.
source: Proteomic studies on three independent particle and plasma membrane preparations revealed that both were enriched in focal adhesion proteins and cytoskeletal components (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: Supported by proteomic analysis results shown in Figure 5.

claim: When analyses were confined to the top 75th percentile of proteins by spectral count, we identified 653 proteins in the particle preparations and 715 proteins in the plasma membrane preparations, with 502 proteins in common.
source: When analyses were confined to the top 75th percentile of proteins by spectral count, we identified 653 proteins in the particle preparations and 715 proteins in the plasma membrane preparations, with 502 proteins in common (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by Venn diagram in Figure 5C.

claim: The top 15 focal adhesion–related proteins, as annotated by Gene Ontology, were found in both the particle and the plasma membrane preparations, but the majority of those proteins were relatively more abundant in the particle preparations.
source: The top 15 focal adhesion–related proteins, as annotated by Gene Ontology, were found in both the particle and the plasma membrane preparations, but the majority of those proteins were relatively more abundant in the particle preparations (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by bar graph in Figure 5D showing protein abundance.

claim: Focal adhesion kinase (FAK) is important for focal adhesion disassembly.
source: Focal adhesion kinase (FAK) is important for focal adhesion disassembly.
evidence: This is established knowledge about FAK function.

claim: Phosphorylation of Tyr-397 in FAK is one of the events in initiating focal adhesion disassembly.
source: Phosphorylation of Tyr-397 in FAK is one of the events in initiating focal adhesion disassembly (Hamadi et al., 2005; Nagano et al., 2012), and that step can be blocked with an FAK inhibitor.
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: In macrophages treated with an FAK inhibitor, the filopodia and lamellipodia remain mobile.
source: In macrophages treated with an FAK inhibitor, the filopodia and lamellipodia remain mobile (Figure 6—videos 1–2).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging videos.

claim: The lawns of particles outside of FAK inhibitor–treated macrophages were ~twice the size of the macrophage cell body, whereas they were only ~40% as large as the cell body in DMSO-treated macrophages.
source: Indeed, the lawns of particles outside of FAK inhibitor–treated macrophages were ~twice the size of the macrophage cell body, whereas they were only ~40% as large as the cell body in DMSO-treated macrophages (10 macrophages were analyzed per group).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of SEM images.

claim: Cholesterol-loaded macrophages retained their mobility, as judged by live-cell imaging.
source: Cholesterol-loaded macrophages (loaded with an incubation with acetylated low-density lipoproteins) retained their mobility, as judged by live-cell imaging (Figure 6—videos 3–4), and lawns of particles were present on the substrate surrounding cholesterol-loaded cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging videos.

claim: When cholesterol-loaded macrophages were treated with an FAK inhibitor, large lawns of particles were observed around almost every cell.
source: When cholesterol-loaded macrophages were treated with an FAK inhibitor, large lawns of particles were observed around almost every cell (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by SEM images in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: STED microscopy revealed avid ALO-D4, but not OlyA, binding to the lawn of particles around macrophages.
source: Stimulated emission depletion (STED) microscopy revealed avid ALO-D4, but not OlyA, binding to the lawn of particles around macrophages (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by STED microscopy images in Figure 6.

claim: The lawn of particles surrounding cells was larger in cells that had been treated with an FAK inhibitor, consistent with the SEM findings.
source: The lawn of particles surrounding cells was larger in cells that had been treated with an FAK inhibitor, consistent with the SEM findings in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.
evidence: Supported by comparison of STED images in Figure 6 with SEM images.

claim: When latrunculin A was added to the medium after allowing the cells to adhere to the substrate ('post-adherence'), a circumferential ring of ALO-D4 binding, but not OlyA binding, was observed on the substrate surrounding macrophages.
source: However, when latrunculin A was added to the medium after allowing the cells to adhere to the substrate ('post-adherence'), a circumferential ring of ALO-D4 binding, but not OlyA binding, was observed on the substrate surrounding macrophages (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), corresponding to the circumferential ring of particles detected by SEM in Figure 2A.
evidence: Supported by STED microscopy images in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Fluorescence microscopy of macrophages that had been incubated with Alexa Fluor 488–labeled [15N]ALO-D4 and mCherry-tagged lysenin revealed avid binding of ALO-D4, but not mCherry-tagged lysenin, to the lawn of particles surrounding macrophages.
source: Indeed, fluorescence microscopy of macrophages that had been incubated with Alexa Fluor 488–labeled [15N]ALO-D4 and mCherry-tagged lysenin (which binds sphingomyelin) revealed avid binding of ALO-D4, but not mCherry-tagged lysenin, to the lawn of particles surrounding macrophages (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy images in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: When macrophages or CHO cells were treated with sphingomyelinase, the binding of OlyA and lysenin to cells was markedly reduced or abolished.
source: When macrophages or CHO cells were treated with sphingomyelinase, the binding of OlyA and lysenin to cells was markedly reduced or abolished (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy images in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: NanoSIMS images revealed that [15N]ALO-D4 bound strongly to the lawn of particles around macrophages; 15N enrichment was ~twofold higher in the lawn of particles than over the cell body.
source: NanoSIMS images revealed that [15N]ALO-D4 bound strongly to the lawn of particles around macrophages; 15N enrichment was ~twofold higher in the lawn of particles than over the cell body (Figure 8D).
evidence: Supported by NanoSIMS quantification in Figure 8D.

claim: 13C enrichment in the lawn of particles (from [13C]OlyA binding) was very low.
source: 13C enrichment in the lawn of particles (from [13C]OlyA binding) was very low (Figures 7 and 8D, Figure 7—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: Supported by NanoSIMS images and quantification.

claim: In the case of [15N]ALO-D4, we observed a fine linear band of 15N enrichment at the extreme outer edge of the cell (~40% greater 15N enrichment than over the cell body).
source: In the case of [15N]ALO-D4, we observed a fine linear band of 15N enrichment at the extreme outer edge of the cell (~40% greater 15N enrichment than over the cell body) (Figures 7 and 8B–D, Figure 7—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: Supported by NanoSIMS images and quantification.

claim: In the case of [13C]OlyA, a broad band of 13C enrichment was observed close to the outer edge of the cell (~60% higher 13C enrichment than over the main body of the cell).
source: In the case of [13C]OlyA, a broad band of 13C enrichment was observed close to the outer edge of the cell (~60% higher 13C enrichment than over the main body of the cell) (Figures 7 and 8B–D, Figure 7—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: Supported by NanoSIMS images and quantification.

claim: The broad band of 13C enrichment corresponded to the lamellipodia of macrophages, visible in the SEM images as well as in the 12C–, 12C14N–, and 32S– NanoSIMS images.
source: The broad band of 13C enrichment corresponded to the lamellipodia of macrophages, visible in the SEM images (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplements 1–2) as well as in the 12C–, 12C14N–, and 32S– NanoSIMS images (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by correlative SEM and NanoSIMS imaging.

claim: By confocal microscopy, the binding of OlyA at the outer edge of the cell overlapped with the binding of phalloidin to the actin cytoskeleton–rich lamellipodia.
source: By confocal microscopy, the binding of OlyA at the outer edge of the cell overlapped with the binding of phalloidin to the actin cytoskeleton–rich lamellipodia (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: The fine linear band of 15N enrichment at the outer edge of the cell extended beyond the broad band of 13C enrichment, as shown by composite images formed from 15N/14N and 13C/12C ratio images.
source: Interestingly, the fine linear band of 15N enrichment at the outer edge of the cell extended beyond the broad band of 13C enrichment, as shown by composite images formed from 15N/14N and 13C/12C ratio images (Figure 8B–C).
evidence: Supported by composite NanoSIMS images in Figure 8B–C.

claim: The FAK inhibitor did not induce any changes to the patterns of [15N]ALO-D4 and [13C]OlyA binding to particles on the substrate or the macrophage cell body.
source: The FAK inhibitor did not induce any changes to the patterns of [15N]ALO-D4 and [13C]OlyA binding to particles on the substrate or the macrophage cell body (Figure 7—figure supplement 4–6).
evidence: Supported by NanoSIMS images in Figure 7—figure supplements 4–6.

claim: Compared with cells that had been incubated with DMSO alone, more [3H]cholesterol was retained within the blebbistatin-treated macrophages.
source: Compared with cells that had been incubated with DMSO alone, more [3H]cholesterol was retained within the blebbistatin-treated macrophages (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A), and there was less [3H]cholesterol in the particle fraction (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by scintillation counting data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The LXR agonist reduced the amount of [3H]cholesterol in macrophages and increased the amount of [3H]cholesterol in the particle fraction.
source: The LXR agonist had the opposite effect, reducing the amount of [3H]cholesterol in macrophages and increasing the amount of [3H]cholesterol in the particle fraction (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by scintillation counting data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: HDL markedly increased efflux of [3H]cholesterol into the cell culture medium.
source: As expected, HDL markedly increased efflux of [3H]cholesterol into the cell culture medium (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by scintillation counting data in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: The macrophages released biotinylated particles, detectable with streptavidin-conjugated 40-nm gold nanoparticles, onto the collagen fibers.
source: The macrophages released biotinylated particles, detectable with streptavidin-conjugated 40-nm gold nanoparticles, onto the collagen fibers (Figure 9A, Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by SEM images in Figure 9A and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: By STED microscopy, binding of ALO-D4 to the lawn of particles on the collagen matrix surrounding macrophages colocalized with streptavidin binding.
source: To test whether the particles were enriched in accessible cholesterol, we plated biotinylated macrophages onto glass coverslips coated with PFA-fixed Alexa Fluor 647–labeled collagen IV and then incubated the cells with Alexa Fluor 488–labeled ALO-D4 and Alexa Fluor 568–labeled streptavidin. By STED microscopy, binding of ALO-D4 to the lawn of particles on the collagen matrix surrounding macrophages colocalized with streptavidin binding (Figure 9B).
evidence: Supported by STED microscopy images in Figure 9B.

claim: The amount of collagen beneath the lawn of particles was depleted, likely reflecting digestion of the collagen IV by the filopodia/lamellipodia of the macrophage.
source: The amount of collagen beneath the lawn of particles was depleted, likely reflecting digestion of the collagen IV by the filopodia/lamellipodia of the macrophage.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on observed collagen depletion in images.

claim: By live-cell microscopy, we observed a live macrophage 'carrying' a dead macrophage, allowing us to observe the projection and retraction of lamellipodia/filopodia over the surface of the dead macrophage.
source: By live-cell microscopy, we observed a live macrophage 'carrying' a dead macrophage, allowing us to observe the projection and retraction of lamellipodia/filopodia over the surface of the dead macrophage (Figure 10—video 1).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging video.

claim: By SEM, we observed release of particles onto both the substrate surrounding the live macrophage and to the surface of the dead macrophage.
source: We then imaged the cells by SEM. By SEM, we observed release of particles onto both the substrate surrounding the live macrophage and to the surface of the dead macrophage (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by SEM images in Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: We observed binding of streptavidin-conjugated gold nanoparticles to the cell body and filopodia of macrophages; however, we also observed binding of streptavidin-conjugated gold nanoparticles to the surface of adjacent endothelial cells.
source: As expected, we observed binding of streptavidin-conjugated gold nanoparticles to the cell body and filopodia of macrophages; however, we also observed binding of streptavidin-conjugated gold nanoparticles to the surface of adjacent endothelial cells (Figure 10).
evidence: Supported by SEM images in Figure 10.

claim: The distribution of gold nanoparticles on the endothelial cells (adjacent to one pole of the macrophage) suggested that plasma membrane–derived biotinylated particles had been released onto the surface of endothelial cells.
source: Nevertheless, the distribution of gold nanoparticles on the endothelial cells (adjacent to one pole of the macrophage) suggested that plasma membrane–derived biotinylated particles had been released onto the surface of endothelial cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the distribution pattern of gold nanoparticles.

claim: The particles on the substrate were derived from the plasma membrane.
source: Our studies with biotinylated macrophages provided further evidence that the particles on the surrounding substrate are derived from the plasma membrane.
evidence: Supported by biotinylation experiments showing plasma membrane markers on particles.

claim: In our studies, the particles on the substrate surrounding macrophages were enriched (relative to the plasma membrane over the cell body) in accessible cholesterol but depleted in sphingomyelin-sequestered cholesterol.
source: In our studies, the particles on the substrate surrounding macrophages were enriched (relative to the plasma membrane over the cell body) in accessible cholesterol but depleted in sphingomyelin-sequestered cholesterol.
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy and NanoSIMS data.

claim: The actin cytoskeleton is tethered, through adaptor proteins, to long acyl-chain–containing phosphatidylserines in the cytoplasmic leaflet of the plasma membrane, which interact with microdomains on the outer leaflet containing cholesterol and long acyl-chain–containing lipids (e.g., sphingolipids).
source: They proposed that the actin cytoskeleton is tethered, through adaptor proteins, to long acyl-chain–containing phosphatidylserines in the cytoplasmic leaflet of the plasma membrane, which interact with microdomains on the outer leaflet containing cholesterol and long acyl-chain–containing lipids (e.g., sphingolipids).
evidence: This is a model proposed by Raghupathy et al., 2015, cited in the text.

claim: According to this model, sphingolipid-associated cholesterol on the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane associates, indirectly, with the actin cytoskeleton and thus would presumably remain tethered to the actin cytoskeleton during movement of filopodia and lamellipodia.
source: According to this model, sphingolipid-associated cholesterol on the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane associates, indirectly, with the actin cytoskeleton and thus would presumably remain tethered to the actin cytoskeleton during movement of filopodia and lamellipodia.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Raghupathy model.

claim: According to this model, the non-sequestered 'accessible' pool of cholesterol, which is known to be mobile, would be more likely than the sphingolipid-sequestered cholesterol to be left behind on the substrate during the movement of filopodia/lamellipodia.
source: According to this model, the non-sequestered 'accessible' pool of cholesterol, which is known to be mobile (Infante and Radhakrishnan, 2017), would be more likely than the sphingolipid-sequestered cholesterol to be left behind on the substrate during the movement of filopodia/lamellipodia.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Raghupathy model and known properties of accessible cholesterol.

claim: We observed broad bands of 13C enrichment along the perimeter of macrophages, corresponding to the broad, flat, actin cytoskeleton–rich lamellipodia, but there was minimal 13C enrichment in the lawn of particles surrounding cells.
source: We observed broad bands of 13C enrichment along the perimeter of macrophages, corresponding to the broad, flat, actin cytoskeleton–rich lamellipodia, but there was minimal 13C enrichment in the lawn of particles surrounding cells.
evidence: Supported by NanoSIMS imaging data.

claim: Both the lawn of particles on the substrate as well as the extreme edge of the macrophage plasma membrane (from which particles are released) were enriched in 15N.
source: In contrast, both the lawn of particles on the substrate as well as the extreme edge of the macrophage plasma membrane (from which particles are released) were enriched in 15N.
evidence: Supported by NanoSIMS imaging data.

claim: The thin linear band of 15N enrichment at the far edge of the cell extends beyond the broad band of [13C]OlyA binding.
source: The thin linear band of 15N enrichment at the far edge of the cell extends beyond the broad band of [13C]OlyA binding.
evidence: Supported by NanoSIMS imaging data.

claim: The plasma membrane at the far edge of the cell is enriched in accessible cholesterol.
source: Thus, the plasma membrane at the far edge of the cell is enriched in accessible cholesterol.
evidence: This is an inference based on 15N enrichment from ALO-D4 binding.

claim: The negligible amounts of 13C enrichment in the lawn of particles around macrophages is explained by the low amounts of 13C within the thin 15N-enriched region at the far edge of the plasma membrane.
source: Presumably, the negligible amounts of 13C enrichment in the lawn of particles around macrophages is explained by the low amounts of 13C within the thin 15N-enriched region at the far edge of the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is an inference based on NanoSIMS data.

claim: Schmidt et al. (1993) described the ripping away of integrin-containing, cytoskeletal element–free membranous particles from rat fibroblasts during cell migration, but those particles (visible by light microscopy) were larger than we observed by SEM around cultured macrophages.
source: For example, Schmidt et al. (1993) described the ripping away of integrin-containing, cytoskeletal element–free membranous particles from rat fibroblasts during cell migration, but those particles (visible by light microscopy) were larger than we observed by SEM around cultured macrophages.
evidence: Comparison with prior literature.

claim: Regen and Horwitz (1992) described release of trails of membranous particles from migrating chicken fibroblasts, but again, the particles were larger than we observed in macrophages.
source: Regen and Horwitz (1992) described release of trails of membranous particles from migrating chicken fibroblasts, but again, the particles were larger than we observed in macrophages.
evidence: Comparison with prior literature.

claim: Vedhachalam et al. (2007) provided suggestive electron microscopy evidence for the protrusion of cholesterol-rich exovesicular domains from the surface of J774 macrophages, but they did not describe the release of vesicular particles from those cells.
source: Vedhachalam et al. (2007) provided suggestive electron microscopy evidence for the protrusion of cholesterol-rich exovesicular domains from the surface of J774 macrophages, but they did not describe the release of vesicular particles from those cells.
evidence: Comparison with prior literature.

claim: Li Yu's group described release of 'migrasomes' from filopodia in a variety of cell lines during cell migration.
source: Most recently, Li Yu's group described release of 'migrasomes' from filopodia in a variety of cell lines during cell migration (Ma et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2019).
evidence: Comparison with prior literature.

claim: Migrasomes were described as cholesterol-rich micron-sized structures that, by electron microscopy, contained multiple 50–100-nm vesicular structures.
source: Migrasomes were described as cholesterol-rich micron-sized structures that, by electron microscopy, contained multiple 50–100-nm vesicular structures.
evidence: Description of migrasomes from prior literature.

claim: Migrasome formation was blocked by cholesterol depletion.
source: Migrasome formation was blocked by cholesterol depletion.
evidence: Finding from prior literature on migrasomes.

claim: In our studies, we did not observe structures resembling migrasomes within the filopodia of cultured macrophages.
source: In our studies, we did not observe structures resembling migrasomes within the filopodia of cultured macrophages.
evidence: Observation from current study.

claim: In an earlier study, we observed lawns of particles surrounding macrophages even after depleting the cells of cholesterol with an overnight incubation with HDL.
source: Also, in an earlier study (He et al., 2018), we observed lawns of particles surrounding macrophages even after depleting the cells of cholesterol with an overnight incubation with HDL.
evidence: Reference to prior work by the authors.

claim: We did find that macrophages are capable of releasing plasma membrane–derived particles onto more physiologic substrates (e.g., collagen matrix, dead cells), lending plausibility to the notion that particle release could occur in vivo.
source: However, we did find that macrophages are capable of releasing plasma membrane–derived particles onto more physiologic substrates (e.g., collagen matrix, dead cells), lending plausibility to the notion that particle release could occur in vivo.
evidence: Supported by experiments showing particle release on collagen and dead cells.
